Let’s dive into Chapter 5: Overcoming the Perfection Trap and the Urge to Please.
If you’ve ever found yourself caught up in trying to do everything flawlessly or feeling like you need to keep everyone happy, you’re definitely not alone. These habits usually come from a good place—maybe you want to do your best, or you care about your relationships. But sometimes, they can actually hold you back at work.
Let’s start with the perfection trap. This is that feeling that every single thing you do needs to be absolutely perfect. Maybe it’s because you grew up with high expectations, or maybe you just really want to avoid criticism. Striving for excellence is great, but here’s something to watch out for: when perfectionism takes over, it can end up causing more stress, making you work way too many hours, and even keeping you from grabbing new opportunities. You might find it tough to pass work to others or to take risks—because, honestly, what if you make a mistake?
In a professional setting, perfectionism can be a bit of a double-edged sword. Sure, it helps you build a reputation for quality and reliability. But it can also mean you miss deadlines, hesitate to try new things, or struggle to step into leadership roles. Leaders, after all, are constantly dealing with tough choices and a fair bit of uncertainty. They need to be able to handle ambiguity and learn from mistakes along the way.
So, how do you move past perfectionism? Here are a few strategies you might find helpful:
First, try setting realistic standards for yourself. Not every task needs the same level of detail or attention.
Next, prioritize your work—focus on what’s truly important and what will have the biggest impact.
Practice a little self-compassion. Remember, mistakes aren’t failures—they’re chances to learn and grow.
And don’t be afraid to delegate. Trusting others with tasks can lighten your load and let you focus on what matters most.
Now, let’s talk about the urge to please. Many women, in particular, are taught to be accommodating and to avoid disappointing anyone. In the workplace, this can mean saying yes to every single request, piling on responsibilities, and putting your own goals on the back burner. Over time, this adds up to burnout and even resentment.
Learning how to set boundaries—and being able to say no when you need to—is absolutely critical. This doesn’t mean you need to stop being helpful or caring. It’s about making intentional choices about where you put your time and energy. You can’t please everyone, and that’s okay. Focusing on what matters to you is key for your own growth.
So what can help with this? Here are some practical strategies:
Start by getting clear on your personal and professional priorities. What’s really important to you?
Practice assertive communication—speak up about your needs and limits, and do it in a way that’s both clear and respectful.
It can also help to get feedback from trusted colleagues. Sometimes, an outside perspective makes it easier to know when you should say yes—and when it’s okay to decline.
And don’t forget to reflect on how overcommitting affects you. If you notice you’re stretched too thin, make adjustments as needed.
By working through these habits, you can create a work life that feels more sustainable and a lot more rewarding. Letting go of perfectionism and the need to please opens up new opportunities, builds your resilience, and helps you feel more in control of your own path.
